list.listitem: Consider the diagnosis of Behcet’s disease in patients with mucocutaneous lesions. Diagnosis is based upon the clinical criteria of the International Study Group. C

Treatment depends on the clinical presentation. Potentially useful drugs include apremilast, topical and systemic steroids, azathioprine, cyclosporin A, thalidomide, colchicine, and tumor necrosis factor inhibitors like adalimumab and infliximab.C
Apremilast has been shown to reduce the number of oral ulcers and improve quality of life scores. B
The main aim of therapy is to reduce the inflammation using immunosuppressives to protect the affected organs like the eye, CVS, or neurological systems. C

background.definition: Behcet's disease (BD) or Bech is a chronic, relapsing multi-system vasculitis of unknown etiology, characterized by oral (aphthous ulcers), genital ulcers, uveitis, and skin lesions with a relapsing and remitting course. Less common manifestations include the involvement of CNS, GI, and large vessels. These involvements may present alone or coexist with certain combinations of systems known as disease phenotypes . It is sometimes called "Silk Road disease".

list.listitem: BD affects younger population (20–40 years) the most. BD is more common along the ancient silk road, extending from the Mediterranean basin to eastern Asia.
In the US, the incidence is about 0.12 to 0.33 per 100,000 and in Turkey, it is 80 to 420 cases per 100,000 population. In eastern Asia (Japan, Korea, China), it is 1.5 to 20/100,000.
A UK study found a prevalence of 15/100,000 population in 2017.
BD shows some female predominance in eastern Asia, while males are frequently affected in the Middle East. Men tend to have more severe symptoms.

The etiology of BD is unknown. It is thought to be multi-factorial with some genetic predisposition. Various environmental factors are implicated as etiology. The disease tend to be less severe after 20 years in many patients. Microbiological agents and their proteins are also implicated.
The most common pathological finding is vasculitis involving arteries and veins of all sizes, excessive neutrophil activation, and auto immune activation.
Presence of vasculitis in noted near the typical lesions (genital ulcers, erythema nodosum, and CNS lesions) of BD.
The vasculitis is associated with hypercoagulability. It is absent in the skin reactions and the CNS lesions.
The diagnosis of BD is clinical, and should be suspected in patients with mucocutaneous ulcers, especially if seen in combination with other typical systemic symptoms. C
Use International Study Group for Behçet's Disease Criteria for the diagnosis of BD. C

Differential.Differential_Features: Inflammatory halo surrounding a yellowish, round ulcer. Systemic manifestations are absent
Respond to folate and severe, multiple ulcers
Arthritis, livido reticularis, migraines, thrombocytopenia, and leukopenia
Butterfly shaped rash worse with sun, oral ulcers, and hair loss
Sinusitis, fever without known cause, fatigue, night sweats, malaise, and chronic ear infections
Fever, sweats, muscle and joint aches, weight loss
Erythema nodosum, Uveitis and genital ulcers
Optic neuritis, spinal fluid finding, MRI finding
Blisters with corneal involvement, no uveitis or thrombophlebitis

list.listitem: The International Study Group’s definition of BD include all of the following: Recurrent oral ulceration (at least three times in 1 year). Two or more of the following four conditions: recurrent genital ulceration, ocular inflammation, defined skin lesions, or a positive pathergy test. The absence of other clinical explanation.

BD is a rare systemic vasculitis of unknown etiology charecterised by recurrent episodes of orogenital ulcers and ocular lesions. It is a multisystem disease, and the diagnosis is primarily clinical. The history should be directed to presence of mucocutaneous ulcers in the past (especially last 3 years), duration of ulcer, presence of pain, presence of scars, and nodular or papulopustular lesions in the skin. Also ask about a history of blurry vision, red eye, or ocular pain. Patients should be asked for cardiovascular symptoms and past history of DVT’s. GI symptoms questioned should include abdominal pain and diarrhea. Patients should be questioned about arthritis, arthralgia, and myalgia symptoms. CNS evaluation should include prior history of neuropathy, CVA, TIA, and recent emotional changes.

Physical examination should include a general examination and a focal examination of mouth, genital region, skin, and a complete CNS examination. Eye examination should include fundoscopic and slit lamp examination. Cardiovascular examination including heart and peripheral vassals should be noted. Abdominal examination should focus on distended veins of the abdomen, masses or pulsation, and other signs of IVC thrombosis.

Mucocutaneous lesions: mucocutaneous lesions are the most common finding. Ulcers are painful and are typically round with a well-defined erythematous border. Lesions in the eye, CNS, and vascular system carry higher morbidity and mortality. Mucocutaneous lesions are the most common presentation of BD and may appear years before other organ involvement. Oral lesions with multiple minor aphthous ulcers (<10 mm) are common (85%), while herpetiform ulcers are less common. Genital ulcers in men usually present in the scrotum; other involvement is less common. In women, they frequently present in the labia majora and minora and less frequently in the cervix and vagina. The lesions are not accompanied by dysuria or discharge as in Reiter's syndrome. It is rarely present in extragenital areas like breast and axilla. The lesions heal in 2 to 4 weeks and the small lesions leave no scar whereas the larger ones may leave a scar.

Skin lesions: papulopustular and nodular lesions (including erythema nodosum) are the most common presentation of BD, occurring in about half of patients, and are more common in women. These lesions are present in the lower extremities and are numerous and leave pigmentation with healing. It is rare in the upper extremity. Acneiform nodules are the classical skin presentation of BD and present in face and chest (like acne). Other lesions (vasculitis, pyoderma gangrenosum, ulcers in the axillary and interdigital areas, Sweet’s syndrome) are less common.

The pathergy reaction of the skin is a non-specific hyper-reactivity reaction to trauma or needle injury. This phenomenon is used in the pathergy test for BD. When this test is positive, BD is highly likely. This reactivity is population dependent: patients from Turkey and Japan have a higher incidence (60%–70%) than northern European population (5%).

Eye: ocular involvement is noted in 50% of patients with BD and usually develops within 3 years of the onset of the disease. Chronic, relapsing bilateral uveitis involving both anterior and posterior chambers of the eye is a common presentation. Acute anterior uveitis with severe inflammation (hypopyon) is uncommon. Posterior uveal inflammation with retinal involvement is rare. Recurrent inflammation may lead to chronic changes and loss of vision if untreated. During the acute phase, it may present with hemorrhagic and exudative retinal lesions of the retina or cellular infiltration of the vitreous humor. Fluorescein angiography is a diagnostic tool for evaluation. The retinal finding may be mistaken for sarcoidosis.

CNS: CNS involvement is found in 5% to 10% of patients; 80% of patents show signs of parenchymal involvement (mainly pyramidal, cerebellar, sensory dysfunction, behavioral changes encephalitis, aseptic meningitis). Non-parenchymal disease includes intracranial hypertension (due to dural venous thrombosis) and peripheral neuropathy.

GI involvement: GI involvement is more common (about 30%) among Japanese patients when compared with Turkish patients. Mucosal ulcerations (usually in the ileum) cause vomiting, dyspepsia, abdominal pain, and diarrhea. Hepatic symptoms may be due to Budd-Chiari syndrome. Use biopsy to distinguish from Crohn’s disease or ulcerative colitis.

Cardiovascular: vascular (both arterial and venous) involvement is more common in men. DVT is more common, including in the vena cava and superficial thrombophlebitis. Arterial involvement is uncommon (5%). Aneurysms of various arteries are common but cardiac involvement is rare.1

Musculoskeletal lesions: joint disease (50% develop arthritis and arthralgias) is very common. Mono or oligoarticular involvement, most commonly in the knee, is most common. Chronic changes may develop into osteonecrosis occasionally. Synovial inflammation and myositis are also common.
Other presentations include renal disease (glomerulonephritis), systemic vasculitis, epididymitis, and voiding dysfunctions.

Anemia and leucocytosis are noted in 15% of patients. ESR and CRP and other inflamatory markers may be moderately elevated and do not correlate with the disease activity. There is some evidence of increased immunoglobulins; there is no increase in autoantibodies such as rheumatoid factor, ANA, or anticardiolipin, and antineutrophilic antibodies (ANCA).

The pathergy test is a valuable diagnostic criterion and it is used to identify skin hyperreactivity to dermal trauma. This test involves pricking (≈0.5 cm depth) the skin with a 20-gauge sterile needle and eliciting hyperreactivity in the form of an erythematous nodule or sterile pustule that is more than 2 mm in diameter at 24 to 48 hours. The sensitivity of pathergy test is only 50% but it has good specificity.

Consider MRI of the brain if CNS lesions are suspected. Lumbar puncture may be needed to differentiate similar conditions (e.g., multiple sclerosis). BD may present with elevated CSF proteins and with pleocytosis. Colonoscopy is indicated for the evaluation of GI symptoms.

The treatment of BD depends upon the severity of the signs and symptoms, age of the patient, sex of the patient, and the systems involved. Patients should be referred to a center with expertise in management of the condition, if possible. C
Corticosteroids (topical or oral) are the mainstay of therapy, along with selective use of azathioprine, colchicine, thalidomide, and TNF inhibitors.C
Cyclosporine and azathioprine protect against eye complications and benzathine penicillin is effective in arthritis. A
Apremilast has been shown to reduce the number of oral ulcers and improve quality of life scores. B
Biologics and monoclonal therapy such as adalimumab and infliximab are increasingly used in BD, especially systemic BD and Behcet uveitis.C
Systematic reviews have found good evidence for the use of azathioprine and cyclosporin A in patients with eye involvement, and interferon alpha for mucocutaneous involvement.

A Phase 2 randomized trial compared apremilast (a phosphodiesterase 4 inhibitor) 30 mg twice daily with placebo for 12 weeks. It reduced the number of ulcer-days (129 vs 222) but caused diarreha, nausea and headache. A Phase 3 trial with 207 patients similarly found fewer oral ulcers in patients treated with apremilast, and a greater improvement in the Behcet Disease Quality of Life Score.

Glucocorticoids are the main therapy for BD complications, but have not been studied in controlled trials. They are primarily used when patients have cardiovascular, GI, CNS, or other large vessel related symptoms. Other agents commonly used include interferon-alpha, thalidomide, colchicines, dapsone, and methotrexate. Biologics such as adalimumab and infliximab are increasingly being used, although clinical trials are lacking and most of the evidence comes from uncontrolled case series.

In a systematic review of ten observational studies of adalimumab for Behcet uveitis, an association between use of adalimumab and improvements in measures of inflammation, macular thickness, and corticosteroid dosage were observed. Six observational non-randomized studies compared adalimumab with infliximab for Behcet uveitis and found comparable efficacy and safety.

A randomized trial of 111 patients with BD who had at least 2 oral ulcers randomized them to 30 mg apremilast (an oral phosphodiesterase-4 inhibitor) or placebo for 3 months. This short-term study found a significant reduction in the number of ulcers at the end of the study (0.5 vs 2.1, p < 0.001).
The following therapies have not been well studied in clinical trials but are often recommended:

Mucocutaneous lesions: Topical steroids and mouth washes are often recommended for milder symptoms. Colchicine has been reported in a small case series to successfully treat mucocutaneous oral and genital lesions, as well as erythema nodosum. Dapsone has also been used for the treatment of erythema nodosum. Thalidomide was somewhat effective in a small controlled trial for mucocutaneous lesions. Other commonly used drugs for more severe oral or genital ulceration include azathioprine and infliximab (Remicade).
Methotrexate is used for mucocutaneous, neurological, articular or opthalmic manfestations of BD, although clinical trials are lacking.

A small, uncontrolled study of 18 patients suggests that inflixmab may be effective for the treatment of intestinal, neurologic and vascular BD who had a poor response or intolerance to conventional therapy.
Erythema nodosum: oral corticosteroids and colchicine are recommended for more severe lesions.
GI lesions are generally treated with sulfasalazine, azathioprine, systemic steroids, or TNF inhibitors.
CNS disease is aggressively treated with systemic corticosteroids, oral azathioprine, or the combination. Cyclophosphamide and chlorambucil have also been proposed.

Eye lesions are managed with multiple medications. Posterior uveitis is treated with oral azathioprine, oral cyclosporine A, or both in combination with oral prednisone. Anterior uveitis is treated with topical mydriatics and local steroid eye drops. Infliximab may be beneficial in resistant pan uveitis. A small case series of patients with severe refractory ophthalmic BD reported favorable outcomes for patients treated with interferon alpha-2a. Two small retrospecctive case series found improvement from baseline in patients given adalimumab or infliximab for uveitis caused by BD.
Joint lesions can be treated with acetaminophen and NSAIDs if symptoms are mild, or colchicine, steroids, or azathioprine for more severe symptoms.
Tumor necrosis factor inhibitors have been proposed for the treatment of patients with Behcet’s based on case reports and small case series. They include etanercept and infliximab.
BD is generally treated medically. Surgical intervention may be necessary in the management of major arterial diseases including aneurysms.
Patients need hospitalization for cardiovascular complications including large-vessel thrombosis, aneurysms, severe CNS conditions, or GI complications.

The prognosis is unpredictable. The outcome and mortality is worse in young men. Those having neurological and eye involvements have increased morbidity. Overall mortality in one study was 9.8%, with most of the morbidity occurring early in the course of the disease.B
Patients with ocular lesions may become blind (about 1 in 4). B

A case-control study of 1281 patients with Behcet disease anbd 5124 matched controls found an increased risk of ischemic heart disease (adjusted hazard ratio 3.1), venous thrombosis (aHR 4.8) and death (aHR 1.4, 95% CI 1.1 - 1.8).
BD is generally mild in elderly when compared with older patients.
Remission is common during pregnancy. About 20% of the patients with pregnancy may experience exacerbation. There are reports of transient neonatal involvement in some patients.
BD is uncommon in children. It affects both sexes equally and mostly presents with recurrent fever. Other manifestations are similar to adults with less frequent eye involvement.
